newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Cetes rates break streak, rise on peso.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Cetes rates break streak, rise on peso.

text.p: After falling to their lowest levels since the 1994 peso crash, rates on Mexican Treasuries rebounded sharply on Tuesday in a move widely expected by the market following last week's peso jitters.
The bellwether 28-day Cetes shot up 257 basis points to 21.16 percent, snapping a 10-week streak of falling rates on growing cheer about the economy's recovery crisis.

Rates at most maturities rose slightly less than expected according to a survey of local dealers by Reuters, which forecasted a rise of 303 basis points in the one-month paper. One year paper rose slightly more than expected.
Economists welcomed the correction in rates, which some said had fallen to negative territory in real terms during February.

"This was no surprise and is very healthy for the market. Looking back, we can see that the 28-day paper especially had fallen too far," Hector Chavez, an economist at Santander Investment in Mexico City, told Reuters.
Rates had fallen sharply in the first weeks of the year as capital inflows from foreign investors kept the peso strong and inflation began to fall after a December holiday peak.

But last week things began to unwind. Fears the peso was getting too strong, plus rising long-term U.S. interest rates on inflation worries, knocked down the currency about two percent. The peso jitters dampened enthusiasm for Mexican paper and drove secondary money market rates sharply higher.
The key question for economists was whether rates might continue to rise or if the correction had ended and rates were high enough to stabilise the peso and attract dollars anew.

"This is probably not the end of the correction. Secondary market rates are still higher and once uncertainty starts it is hard to stop," said Francisco Blanco, an economist at Arka Brokerage in Mexico City.
Overnight Cetes rates ended at 22.80 percent on Tuesday.

Chavez agreed, saying it was unlikely rates would begin to fall again during March, a month when local players like to cover their dollar positions ahead of Holy Week. He said the March 25 meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve would also keep pressure on rates.
Some market watchers said the market was also likely to get jittery during the run-up to key mid-term elections in early July.
Economists added the U.S. bond market will be a key factor in whether or not investors regain an appetite for Mexican securities.
On the plus side, demand picked back up this week after falling sharply in recent weeks. Demand was 12.06 billion pesos compared to 7.82 billion the week before.
